title: The Second Letter to the Corinthians
subtitle: Pros Korinthious B, “Second to the Corinthians”
description: The most personal of Paul’s letters, written after a painful visit and a letter written with many tears, to a church he loved and that had hurt him. Here is the God from whom all comfort comes; a ministry not of the written letter but of the Spirit, with faces uncovered, changed from glory to ever greater glory; treasure in pots made of clay; the message of reconciliation and a new creation in Christ; the grace of the Lord who, rich as he was, became poor; and, against rivals who boasted of their strength, an apostle who boasted of his weakness, a thorn in the flesh, and the answer “My grace is enough for you.” In the Open Word Bible, a new translation from the Greek given freely to the public domain, with an introduction to the letter’s shape and meaning and a conclusion on where to read next.

qa.question: What is 2 Corinthians?
qa.answer: The eighth book of the New Testament, a letter from the apostle Paul to the church in Corinth, written after 1 Corinthians. It celebrates a reconciliation between Paul and the church after a painful break, prepares them for a collection for the poor believers in Jerusalem, and defends Paul’s ministry against rival teachers. Its great theme is that God’s power is seen in human weakness: “it is when I am weak that I am strong” (12:10).

qa.question: Who wrote 2 Corinthians, and when?
qa.answer: The apostle Paul, together with Timothy, who is named in the first verse. Scholars of every school agree that Paul wrote it. He sent it from Macedonia, in northern Greece, probably around AD 55–56, after Titus had brought him the news that the Corinthians had repented and longed to see him again (7:5–7).

qa.question: What happened between 1 and 2 Corinthians?
qa.answer: The letter itself suggests the outline, though details are uncertain. Paul made a painful visit to Corinth (2:1), where someone wronged him; he then wrote a severe letter “with many tears” (2:4), now usually called the tearful letter, and sent it with Titus. Anxious for news, he left Troas for Macedonia, where Titus met him with good news (2:12–13, 7:5–16). Meanwhile, rival teachers had arrived in Corinth, whom Paul answers in chapters 10–13.

qa.question: Is 2 Corinthians one letter or several?
qa.answer: Christians and scholars differ. The tone changes sharply at chapter 10, chapters 8 and 9 both deal with the collection, and 6:14–7:1 seems to interrupt its context, so many scholars think the book joins two or more of Paul’s letters to Corinth, perhaps with chapters 10–13 as part of the tearful letter or a later one. Others argue that it is a single letter written over some time. No manuscript has it in any other form, and the church has always received it as one book.

qa.question: What was Paul’s thorn in the flesh?
qa.answer: No one knows. Paul says only that “a thorn in the flesh was given” to him, “a messenger of Satan”, to keep him from becoming too proud after a vision of paradise, and that he begged the Lord three times to remove it (12:7–8). Suggestions have included an illness or disability, perhaps of the eyes, persecution, a group of opponents and temptation. What Paul passes on is the Lord’s answer: “My grace is enough for you, for power comes to its fullness in weakness.”

qa.question: Which translation of the Bible is this?
qa.answer: The Open Word Bible, a new translation made directly from the Greek and dedicated to the public domain, printed here at its Balanced level, which aims to be accurate and to read naturally aloud. The reasoning behind each of its sentences, with the Greek beside it, is published at openwordbible.org. The introduction and conclusion were written for this edition.
